Medicines and anti-doping: beta-blockers, TUE, supplements

At championships and major events you may be tested for doping. The international rules come from the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA), which publishes a new Prohibited List each year.

Safety: Beta-blockers are heart medicines that slow the heartbeat and reduce shaking; examples are propranolol, atenolol, bisoprolol and metoprolol. Note that under the WADA Prohibited Lists for 2026 and 2027, beta-blockers are prohibited in shooting at all times, in and out of competition.

The list does not name Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ or Compak® Sporting separately: treat beta-blockers as prohibited there too. Your national anti-doping agency can test at national events, and organisers may apply the WADA list.

They are prohibited in precision sports because a slower heart and less tremor can steady the gun.

Some research

Safety: If a doctor has prescribed you a beta-blocker, for example for blood pressure, heart rhythm, migraine or tremor, do not stop it on your own. Talk to your doctor and your federation well before the competition about a permitted alternative or a TUE.

A TUE (Therapeutic Use Exemption) is official permission to use a prohibited medicine for a medical reason. A prescription alone is not enough: a prohibited substance stays prohibited, so you apply in advance, usually to your national anti-doping agency (your federation can tell you which one).

Check each medicine, including those you buy without a prescription. Global DRO is an online medicine check run by several national anti-doping agencies. It lists only medicines sold in its partner countries, such as the UK, the USA, Canada and Switzerland. Search by the active ingredient; if your medicine is not listed, ask your national anti-doping agency or your federation. Check again each year, because the list changes.

Some cold remedies and ADHD medicines (for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder) contain stimulants, substances that make you more alert. Examples: pseudoephedrine (prohibited above a set amount in your sample) and methylphenidate. Stimulants are prohibited in competition.

“In competition” starts at 23:59 on the day before the event and lasts until the event and any doping test after it are over. So whatever you take from that evening onwards counts as “in competition”.

THC, the active substance in cannabis, is prohibited in competition. CBD is not prohibited, but CBD products can contain THC.

Supplements can be contaminated or wrongly labelled. If you take any, choose products whose maker says, on the pack or website, that each production batch has been tested for banned substances by an independent lab.

Some research

Caffeine is not prohibited; WADA only monitors it. Your usual coffee is fine as far as the rules go.

Note that alcohol has not been on the WADA Prohibited List since 1 January 2018. That is not permission: do not drink before or during shooting, and grounds and national law have their own rules. More in Competition day: sleep, coffee, water and food.

Safety: Some medicines, such as allergy tablets, sedatives, sleeping pills and strong painkillers, can make you drowsy or dizzy. Ask your doctor or pharmacist whether you can shoot and drive with them. If you feel drowsy or dizzy, do not shoot that day.

This lesson was checked against the WADA Prohibited Lists for 2026 and 2027 on 6 October 2026. The 2027 list applies from 1 January 2027.

Key points

  • Beta-blockers are prohibited in shooting at all times; treat them as prohibited in clay shooting too.
  • A prescribed medicine: do not stop it yourself; ask your doctor about an alternative or a TUE well in advance.
  • Check each medicine in Global DRO by its active ingredient, or ask your national anti-doping agency; check again each year.
  • A medicine makes you drowsy or dizzy: ask a doctor, and do not shoot while you feel it.
  • Supplements: only products with lab-tested batches; CBD products can contain THC.

Did you know?

The WADA Prohibited List is updated each year, and the next list is usually published around September. A medicine that was allowed last season is worth checking again.

For the coach
  • Ask new shooters early whether they take any regular medicine, and point them to their doctor and Global DRO. Do not give medical advice yourself.

Check yourself · 3 questions

  1. Under the WADA list, when are beta-blockers prohibited in shooting?

    1. Only on the days of a competition
    2. Only at world and European championships
    3. At all times, in and out of competition
    Answer

    At all times, in and out of competition

    The 2026 and 2027 lists mark shooting as prohibited at all times. Treat this as the rule in clay shooting too.

  2. You need a prescribed medicine and are going to a championship. What should you do?

    1. Check early with your doctor; ask about a TUE
    2. Nothing: a prescription always makes it allowed
    3. Stop taking it before the event on your own
    Answer

    Check early with your doctor; ask about a TUE

    A prohibited substance stays prohibited with a prescription. Do not stop a medicine yourself; ask early about alternatives or a TUE.

  3. Where can you check whether a medicine is prohibited?

    1. On the box the medicine came in
    2. In Global DRO, an online check
    3. With the referee on the day of the event
    Answer

    In Global DRO, an online check

    Global DRO is run by several national anti-doping agencies; search by the active ingredient, and if your medicine is not listed, ask your national anti-doping agency or your federation.

This is not medical advice.
